Dubu Jorim Braised Tofu

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the pan that makes tofu a banchan. Dubu jorim takes the blandest protein on earth and makes it the bowl that disappears first from the vegetarian corner of the table: firm tofu, pan-seared into golden plates, then braised briefly in soy-garlic-sesame until every plate wears the glaze. The technique is the two-stage logic the potato record (#B09) runs in reverse — sear first for structure, braise second for flavor — and it converts tofu skeptics more reliably than any deep fry.

The tofu

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Dry the tofu like you mean it. Paper towel, weight (a plate) for 10 minutes, pat again. Water in the tofu is spitting oil and steamed gray slabs; the pressed slabs sear gold. This is the record's only demanding step and it happens before the stove.
  • If using the radish bed, lay the half-moons flat across the pan floor before the seared slabs return — they braise to sweet transparency underneath and become half the bowl.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    The sear: oil at medium-high, slabs in without touching, 3–4 minutes to deep gold (they release when ready — nudged early, they tear), flip once, 2–3 minutes more, out to a plate. Checkpoint — both faces evenly golden-brown with a firming surface — the crust is the sponge that will drink the braise; a pale slab stays bland no matter how good the sauce.
  2. 02
    Pour off the oil, braise liquids into the pan (water, soy, honey, garlic), radish bed if using, seared slabs back over. Simmer 4–5 minutes at medium-low, spooning the liquid over the slabs twice. Checkpoint — the liquid has reduced to a glossy shallow pool and the slabs' faces have gone from dry-gold to lacquered amber; the tofu, pressed thin before, has visibly drunk.
  3. 03
    Sesame oil off the heat, sesame and scallion over. Checkpoint — the eating test: a slab on rice — savory-sweet glaze, the crust's chew, the soft interior, and the radish (if used) sweet enough to surprise. It should taste like the banchan board's quiet centerpiece, which at a table full of grilled meat is exactly what it is. Chef’s Note — the sear-then-braise order is not negotiable, and the reason is structural: tofu braised from raw absorbs unevenly and falls apart at the turn, while seared tofu has a closed crust with an open interior — flavor enters the faces, structure stays in the slab. The same law, inverted, explains #B09's braise-then-glaze: potato needs the long cook before the short paint. Protein sears first; starch braises first.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Slabs tore at the flipUnder-seared or soft tofuFull golden release; firm (not silken) tofu
Oil spat violentlyWet tofuThe 10-minute press and second pat
Bland interiorsThin slabs, short braise1 cm slabs; the full 5 minutes, spooned twice
Glaze wateryBraise stopped earlyReduce to the shallow glossy pool

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat in the pan 2 minutes with a splash of water. Cold glazed slabs in a lunchbox with rice are a Korean cafeteria staple by right.
  • Variations: gochugaru-dusted braise for the red bowl; the same braise over mushrooms and tofu together; a slice of cheese melted on the hot slab is the school-lunch fork — fusion, labeled, beloved.
